title: Who might benefit from the devolution revolution?
gist: A Resolution Foundation weekly guest-edited by KPMG UK's Yael Selfin argues that Andy Burnham's plan to let combined authorities retain a slice of locally raised income tax is far more attractive to booming tax bases (London +51%, Greater Manchester second) than to weak ones (North East +13%), while core spending power fell 18-23% everywhere — making the redistribution formula, not the devolution principle, the decisive variable. It pairs this with research on labour scarcity driving technology adoption, the limits of copying 'Manchesterism', evidence that US TFP growth is additive rather than exponential, the 'brawn premium' behind the non-graduate gender pay gap, and the local employment gains from international students.

insights.claim: Andy Burnham has promised to let UK combined authorities keep a slice of the income tax raised in their own area, a shift whose appeal depends entirely on the local tax base rather than on the principle of devolution.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Local fiscal retention re-prices UK regional risk: high-growth city-regions gain a structurally stronger revenue base while low-growth regions become more dependent on the redistribution formula still to be published.
insights.quote: Today, Andy Burnham has promised to let combined authorities keep a slice of the income tax raised on their patch, and this week’s chart shows why that idea might be more attractive to some areas than others

insights.claim: Real-terms income tax receipts between 2010/11 and 2023/24 grew 51 per cent in London and just 13 per cent in the North East, with Greater Manchester in second place behind London.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: A near four-fold spread in regional tax-base growth quantifies exactly how unequal the payoff from fiscal devolution would be across UK regions.
insights.quote: London is the extreme case, with receipts up 51 per cent, and Greater Manchester in second place, while the North East saw growth of just 13 per cent.

insights.claim: Local core spending power in England fell by between 18 and 23 per cent in every area including London over 2010/11 to 2023/24, showing that centrally mediated funding has been uniformly squeezed regardless of how fast a region's tax base grew.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: The current system has fully decoupled local revenue growth from local spending; any move to tax retention is therefore a large regime change for municipal credit and service provision, not a marginal tweak.
insights.quote: it fell by between 18 and 23 per cent in every area, London included

insights.claim: The more that local areas retain the tax they raise, the more the design of the redistribution mechanism determines whether devolution narrows or widens regional inequality.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Watch the equalisation/rebalancing detail rather than the headline announcement — it is the single parameter that decides the regional distributional outcome.
insights.quote: Getting that balance right is what will decide whether devolution narrows regional gaps or widens them.
insights.locator: the more that areas keep what they raise

themes.theme: Narrow UK fiscal headroom and the productivity problem

insights.claim: Resolution Foundation estimated the new UK Chancellor's fiscal headroom at about £8 billion, a narrow margin against a backdrop of evolving geopolitical uncertainty.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: An £8bn buffer leaves gilt markets exposed to small forecast revisions and constrains how much any devolution or growth package can be funded up front.
insights.quote: RF estimated that the fiscal headroom for the new Chancellor stood at about £8 billion, quite a narrow margin, especially in the context of evolving geopolitical uncertainty
insights.locator: What has so far received less focus

insights.claim: Sustainable improvements in UK living standards depend on productivity growth, and policymakers cannot rely on AI arriving to solve decades-long underperformance.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: A senior UK economist explicitly discounting an AI-driven productivity rescue is a caution against pricing UK trend growth upgrades off the AI narrative.
insights.quote: We can’t just sit and wait for AI to fix it.
insights.locator: And I am sure I don’t need to remind you

insights.claim: The first two weeks of Andy Burnham's premiership were dominated by a 'cost of living week' followed by trickier policy issues, with the UK's continued economic challenges receiving comparatively little focus.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Political bandwidth is being spent on distributional retail policy rather than the growth agenda, a signal for the composition of upcoming fiscal announcements.
insights.quote: We are now two weeks into Andy Burnham’s premiership – and while last week ended up as ‘cost of living week’, this week has been focused on some of the trickier policy issues.
insights.locator: This is Yael Selfin stepping in as a guest editor

themes.theme: Labour scarcity as the trigger for technology adoption

insights.claim: During the Napoleonic Wars of 1792-1815 over 10 per cent of British working-age men were pulled into the army and navy, creating a natural experiment in labour scarcity.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Provides the historical baseline for arguing that severe labour withdrawal, not technology availability alone, drives mechanisation.
insights.quote: Between 1792 and 1815, over 10 per cent of working-age men were pulled into the army and navy.

insights.claim: Comparing two similar Norfolk parishes 32km apart, the one with water deep enough for the Navy's biggest ships saw twice as many labour-saving threshing machines adopted as the parish on a shallow estuary.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: A clean identification that labour scarcity causes capital deepening — useful for forecasting where AI adoption will concentrate.
insights.quote: the deep-water parish saw twice as many labour-saving threshing machines adopted

insights.claim: Technology adoption was strongest where skilled mechanics were locally available and labour was scarce, meaning complementary skills and tight labour markets are joint preconditions rather than substitutes.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Maps directly onto AI: regions or firms lacking both AI skills and wage pressure should be expected to underinvest, widening dispersion in returns.
insights.quote: Crucially, technology adoption was strongest where skilled mechanics were on hand and with a scarcity of labour.

insights.claim: If workers are abundant rather than scarce, firms' incentives to fully embrace the AI revolution may be diminished, implying loose labour markets slow rather than accelerate AI diffusion.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Cuts against the assumption that AI capex is unconditional: a slack UK labour market could be a genuine brake on enterprise AI adoption and on the associated productivity payoff.
insights.quote: But with workers abundant rather than scarce would that diminish the incentives for firms to fully embrace the AI revolution?
insights.locator: A potential relevance for present day Britain

insights.claim: Since the turn of the millennium the Manchester city-region has been one of the fastest growing outside London, driven largely by expansion of knowledge-intensive and tradable services.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Identifies tradable knowledge services — not manufacturing or public sector expansion — as the actual engine behind the UK's leading non-London regional growth story.
insights.quote: the city-region of Manchester has been one of the fastest growing outside London, with the expansion of knowledge-intensive and tradable services playing a major role

insights.claim: Greater Manchester remains more than a third less productive than London despite being a regional growth success, and its gains have been concentrated in the city centre.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Even the best-performing UK regional model has not closed the London gap, tempering expectations for what devolution-led growth can deliver on national productivity.
insights.quote: But Greater Manchester still remains more than a third less productive than London.

insights.claim: Universities have been central to Manchester attracting talent, but retaining graduates after study remains a challenge for the city-region.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Graduate retention, not graduate production, is the binding constraint on regional human capital — a policy lever distinct from university funding.
insights.quote: though universities have been a big part of attracting talent, retaining graduates remains a challenge

insights.claim: The conditions behind Manchester's success and its appeal to foreign investors are neither universal nor quick to recreate, so replication requires building each city's own institutions and productive potential rather than copying a template.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Undercuts the political shortcut of rolling out a single 'Manchester model' nationally; expect slow, uneven returns from levelling-up style regional programmes.
insights.quote: Replicating ‘Manchesterism’ will mean thinking about other cities’ individual productive potential and helping them to build their institutions, as well as pushing Manchester’s own transformation further.

insights.claim: Growth theory's assumption that productivity compounds — each year's gain proportional to the level already reached — was adopted for mathematical convenience rather than because the evidence supported it.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: If true, long-run growth models and the terminal growth rates embedded in valuations rest on an unexamined functional-form choice.
insights.quote: This paper argues that was always convenience rather than evidence.

insights.claim: US total factor productivity data from 1890 to 2022 shows growth is additive rather than exponential, with TFP rising since 1947 by a near-constant amount each year equal to about 2.5 per cent of its 1947 level.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: A constant absolute increment implies percentage growth must decay over time — a structurally lower long-run growth path than compounding models assume.
insights.quote: since 1947, TFP has risen by a near-constant amount each year – about 2.5 per cent of its 1947 level

insights.claim: Under fixed annual increments the measured productivity growth rate falls mechanically from 2.5 per cent to around 1 per cent over 60 years, so part of the observed productivity slowdown may be an arithmetic artefact rather than a policy failure.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Reframes the UK/US productivity puzzle: if decay is mechanical, policy interventions aimed at restoring 2-3% trend growth are targeting an unattainable benchmark.
insights.quote: We may have misread a straight line as a curve.
insights.locator: If you buy this and apply it to Britain

themes.theme: The 'brawn premium' and the non-graduate gender pay gap

insights.claim: Women are more likely than men to obtain a degree and earn a higher college premium, yet still earn less overall because women without degrees are paid less than non-college men in all 21 OECD countries studied.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Locates the gender pay gap in the non-graduate segment, meaning education-expansion policies alone will not close it.
insights.quote: In all 21 OECD countries studied, women without degrees are paid less than their non-college male counterparts

insights.claim: In the US, occupational differences arising from men's concentration in 'brawn intensive' roles such as truck driving, construction and carpentry explain 42 per cent of the non-college gender pay gap.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Two-fifths of the gap is occupational sorting, so automation of physically intensive trades would materially reshape the gender wage distribution.
insights.quote: They find these differences in occupation explain two-fifths (42 per cent) of the pay gap, suggesting it is a major factor.

insights.claim: ONS data shows the UK gender pay gap is highest in skilled trades, so putting technical skills at the heart of schools risks entrenching the gap unless the new pathways offer equal opportunities to girls and boys.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: A concrete design risk in UK vocational education reform: expanding technical pathways could widen rather than narrow the gender pay gap.
insights.quote: the gender pay gap in the UK was highest for those in skilled trades

themes.theme: International students as local demand and productivity shock

insights.claim: US data from 2003 to 2015 shows one additional international student per thousand working-age residents raises the local employment rate by 0.19 percentage points and average wages by 0.48 per cent.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Quantifies international students as a local demand shock with measurable wage and employment effects, contradicting the framing of them as passive consumers.
insights.quote: one additional international student per thousand working-age residents raises the local employment rate by 0.19 percentage points and average wages by 0.48 per cent

insights.claim: International students raise local wages through spending on housing, groceries and tuition while also intensifying competition that pushes labour toward higher-performing businesses and forces the least productive firms out.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: The mechanism is both demand-side and reallocative, so cutting student inflows hits local productivity as well as local spending.
insights.quote: International students also intensify competition, pushing labour toward higher-performing businesses and forcing the least productive ones out.

insights.claim: Rising foreign enrolment over 2003-2015 may have created around 1.17 million jobs in the US, so tightening immigration policy amid rising trade tensions would impose real costs on local economies.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Puts a jobs number on student-visa restriction — a downside channel for US and UK university towns and regional labour markets if enrolment reverses.
insights.quote: Rising foreign enrolment over the study period may have created around 1.17 million jobs in the US according to the study.
